content: 1. A clinical trial conducted by Yuan Q, Liu L, Ma J, Wu W, Ye M, and Zhang Y in 2021 investigated the effects of acupuncture therapy on chronic nonspecific low back pain. The study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic benefits of acupuncture in managing this condition. 2. Molsberger AF, Mau J, Pawelec DB, and Winkler J conducted a randomized, blinded, controlled trial in 2002 to determine whether acupuncture could improve orthopedic management of chronic low back pain. The study included a three-month follow-up period to assess the outcomes. 3. In 2019, de Castro Moura C, de Cássia Lopes Chaves E, Couto Machado Chianca T, Ruginsk SG, Alves Nogueira D, and Iunes DH examined the effects of auricular acupuncture on chronic pain in adults with back musculoskeletal disorders. This randomized clinical trial focused on the efficacy of auricular acupuncture in reducing pain intensity. 4. Brinkhaus B, Witt CM, Jena S, et al., in 2006, conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of acupuncture in patients with chronic low back pain. The study provided evidence on the potential benefits of acupuncture as a treatment modality. 5. Ushinohama A, Cunha BP, Costa LO, Barela AM, and Freitas PB, in 2016, investigated the impact of a single session of ear acupuncture on pain intensity and postural control in individuals with chronic low back pain. This randomized controlled trial aimed to assess the immediate effects of ear acupuncture. 6. Kerr DP, Walsh DM, and Baxter D conducted a blinded, randomized controlled trial in 2003 to explore the role of acupuncture in managing chronic low back pain. The study provided insights into the clinical utility of acupuncture for this condition. 7. The WHO guideline on the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults includes a summary of evidence-to-decision (EtD) considerations. These guidelines evaluate the benefits and harms of acupuncture in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above, compared to usual care. 8. The guideline also incorporates critical outcomes such as pain reduction, back-specific function/disability, general function/disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, adverse events, changes in medication use, and falls. These outcomes are considered for all adults and older adults. 9. The grading of evidence includes assessments of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations. For example: Risk of bias is categorized as not serious, serious, or very serious based on the proportion of trials with low or high risk of bias. Inconsistency is evaluated based on the similarity of point estimates, overlap of confidence intervals, and statistical heterogeneity (I² values). Indirectness is assessed based on the relevance of the evidence to the population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes (PICO framework). Imprecision is downgraded when sample sizes are small, confidence intervals are wide, or thresholds for clinical importance are crossed. 10. Specific explanations for downgrading evidence include: Performance bias due to lack of patient blinding. High levels of statistical heterogeneity (I² > 75%) with treatment effects in different directions. Small sample sizes or single-center trials that limit generalizability. Selection bias due to unclear treatment allocation or high attrition rates. 11. Spinal manipulative therapy (SMT) is defined as a hands-on treatment involving movement of spinal joints. It includes high-velocity, low-amplitude manipulation and low-velocity, low-amplitude mobilization techniques. Mobilization involves passive movement within the joint's range of motion, while manipulation uses a high-velocity thrust near the end of the range, often accompanied by an audible crack. 12. The WHO guideline also evaluates the benefits and harms of SMT in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above, compared to sham SMT or placebo treatment. 13. The evidence synthesis for SMT includes similar grading criteria as acupuncture, with considerations for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors. For example: Downgrading occurs when trials lack patient blinding, have high attrition rates, or include small sample sizes. Inconsistency is noted when treatment effects vary in direction or confidence intervals show poor overlap. 14. The guideline emphasizes the importance of critical outcomes such as pain reduction, functional improvement, quality of life, and adverse events in evaluating the effectiveness of SMT and acupuncture for chronic low back pain. 15. Judgments on equity, human rights, acceptability, and feasibility are based on the experience of guideline development group (GDG) members, as no evidence synthesis was commissioned for these considerations. 16. The guideline highlights the need for further research to address gaps in evidence, particularly for older adults and specific subgroups, to improve the management of chronic primary low back pain.
